title: Halva Irani
subtitle: Persian saffron halva
excerpt: Halva Irani is a dense, fragrant Persian sweet made by cooking plain flour in butter until golden, then stirring in saffron-infused syrup until it thickens to a fudge-like paste. Serves 6.
sourceNotes: Persian halva differs from sesame-based halva found elsewhere in the Middle East. The flour-based version is distinctly Iranian and is traditionally served at mourning ceremonies and religious occasions.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Halva keeps well at room temperature for 3 days covered with cling film.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dense sweet confection found across the Middle East and Central Asia, made from flour, nuts or sesame, cooked with fat and sweetened syrup.
The dried stigmas of the crocus flower, the world's most expensive spice, giving food a golden colour and a warm floral flavour.

content.text: is made by frying flour in butter until it smells nutty and toasted, then adding a hot
and rose water syrup. The mixture thickens very quickly once the liquid is added. Stir continuously from this point or it will seize. Serves 6.
The finished halva is pressed into a shallow dish and scored into diamonds. It is served at room temperature, not warm, so the texture has a chance to firm up.

items.prepNote: ground and steeped in 2 tbsp hot water

content.text: Make the syrup first. Combine the sugar, water, saffron water, rose water and cardamom in the medium saucepan. Heat over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Bring to a simmer, cook for 3 minutes then remove from the heat and keep warm.

Melt the butter and oil together in the frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the flour and stir continuously with a wooden spoon for 15 to 18 minutes until the flour turns a golden amber colour and smells nutty. Do not stop stirring. Do not let it burn.

Remove the flour from the heat briefly. Carefully and slowly pour the warm syrup into the flour, stirring vigorously as you pour. The mixture will bubble and steam. Return to low heat and stir constantly for 3 to 4 minutes until the halva pulls away from the sides of the pan and forms a thick, smooth paste.
Immediately spread the halva into a shallow greased dish or onto a lined baking tray. Smooth the surface with the back of a wet spoon. Scatter chopped pistachios over the top.
While still warm, score the surface into diamond shapes with a sharp knife. Leave to cool completely at room temperature, about 1 hour, before serving.

attrs.solution: Stir constantly and keep the heat at medium-low. Spots of heat create uneven browning. If the edges are darkening faster than the centre, reduce the heat and keep stirring in circular motions from the edges inward.

attrs.problem: Halva is grainy rather than smooth
attrs.solution: The syrup needs to be warm when added to the flour. Cold syrup causes the mixture to seize into lumps. Keep the syrup on low heat while you toast the flour.

attrs.problem: Halva is too dry and crumbly
attrs.solution: The flour may have been cooked too long. Once the halva is in the dish, press it firmly to compact it. A crumbly halva still tastes correct but will not score into neat diamonds.

content.text: Persian halva is associated with grief and ceremony in Iran. It is made and distributed at funerals, during Muharram and on the anniversary of deaths. The golden colour comes from saffron, the most expensive spice in the world. Iran is the world's largest producer of saffron. The flower-and-cardamom flavour combination is distinctly Persian and not found in other regional halva traditions.
